assessment.name: Adolescent Dissociative Experiences Scale (A-DES)
assessment.description: The Adolescent Dissociative Experiences Scale (A-DES) is a 30-item self-report measure designed to assess both normal and pathological dissociative experiences in adolescents aged 11-18 years (Armstrong et al., 1997 ).

administration.instructions: These questions ask about different kinds of experiences that happen to people. For each question, select the number that tells how much that experience happens to you.

A cutoff score of 4.0 has been suggested for identifying adolescents with pathological dissociation (Kisiel & Lyons, 2001). Based on the available normative data and clinical findings across studies, NovoPsych presents interpretive guidelines for the A-DES. Four severity categories are proposed:

Moderate (3.0-3.9), represents scores exceeding general psychiatric means but falling below the clinical threshold of 4.0, and is similar to means observed in adolescents with psychotic disorders (Armstrong et al., 1997).

High (4.0 and above), consistent with the clinical cutoff suggested by Kisiel and Lyons (2001) and corresponds to mean scores observed in adolescents with dissociative disorders (Armstrong et al., 1997).

When the A-DES score exceeds 4.0, further assessment for a dissociative disorder is recommended, potentially including structured clinical interview. It should be noted that relying strictly on this threshold might miss cases with clinically significant dissociation, as Armstrong et al. (1997) found meaningful dissociative symptoms even in their general psychiatric sample (mean = 2.2). Therefore, considering a reduced cutoff in the Moderate range (3.0-3.9) will yield higher sensitivity, particularly when there is a trauma history or when scores on specific subscales are notably elevated.

source_guidance.title: A-DES Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
The A-DES is scored by calculating the mean of all 30 items, resulting in a total score ranging from 0 to 10. Higher scores indicate greater frequency and severity of dissociative experiences.

The four A-DES subscale scores can be calculated to provide a more nuanced understanding of the adolescent’s dissociative experiences:
1. Dissociative amnesia (items: 2, 5, 8, 12, 15, 22, 27): assesses gaps in memory and awareness.
2. Absorption and imaginative involvement (items 1, 7, 10, 18, 24, 28): measures the tendency to become highly engrossed in activities with reduced awareness of surroundings.
3. Passive influence (items 4, 14, 16, 19, 23): examines experiences of not having volitional control over one’s body and sensations.
4. Depersonalisation and derealization (items 3, 6, 9, 11, 13, 17, 20, 21, 25, 26, 29, 30): reflects feelings of disconnection from one’s body and the world.
NovoPsych have created the following guidelines to assist in interpretation:
Low (0-1.9): Minimal dissociative experiences; typical of non-clinical adolescents.
Mild (2.0-2.9): Some dissociative experiences but generally within normal limits for adolescents.
Moderate (3.0-3.9): Notable dissociative experiences that may indicate elevated risk.
High (4.0 and above): Significant dissociative experiences consistent with clinical levels.
The total score is often expressed as a percentile rank based on normative data from non-clinical adolescent samples. This percentile contextualises the adolescent’s score relative to peers, indicating the percentage of adolescents who scored lower. For example, a score at the 85th percentile means that 85% of adolescents in the normative sample scored lower, placing the individual in the upper range of dissociative experiences.

On first administration a stacked bar graph showing total and subscale average scores is displayed, along with a comparison graph illustrating the client’s scores relative to different reference groups.

When the assessment is administered multiple times, a longitudinal line graph is generated to track changes in the total score.

In addition to a subscale average score graph over time.

When tracking clinical progress, a meaningful change is defined as an increase or decrease of at least half a standard deviation in the total score (approximately .9 points on the 0-10 scale) This criterion is based on the Minimally Important Difference (MID) calculation (Turner et al., 2010). Such changes indicate meaningful improvement or reduction in symptoms, while a change of less than the specified points suggests no meaningful change in symptom severity between assessments. Regular monitoring of A-DES scores can help evaluate treatment effectiveness and guide intervention.
